The study was conducted on the MAR-M 246+Hf nickel-based superalloy.
The furnace temperature gradient was approximately 70°C/cm at the liquidus and 135°C/cm at the solidus.
The magnetic field uniformity was only maintained over a 5 cm region near the center of the pole pieces.
The carbide volume fraction was 25% lower in the magnetic field samples compared to the no-field samples.
The volume fraction of the interdendritic eutectic constituent was 30% higher in the magnetic field samples.
The secondary dendrite arm spacing was 20% larger in the magnetic field samples.
The primary dendrite arm spacing was not significantly affected by the magnetic field.
Microprobe analysis showed reduced chemical segregation in the magnetic field samples.
Experiments were also conducted with cyclic application and removal of the magnetic field.
The shape factor analysis did not provide a reliable method for distinguishing between blocky and script-like carbide morphologies.
The authors note that future experiments should investigate a magnetic field orientation parallel to the gravitational vector.
The study aimed to optimize microstructural features in the MAR-M 246+Hf superalloy through control of the solidification process using a magnetic field.
Directional solidification under low-gravity conditions has also been shown to influence microstructural features in superalloys.
Carbide morphology and distribution can have a significant influence on the mechanical properties of nickel-based superalloys.
Proper control of microstructural features during solidification is a major challenge in the production of superalloy components.
